light.text:
You are standing in the light.

She does not stop working. The hammer comes down, the piece turns, the hammer comes down. A girl of about nine — her daughter — is sorting charcoal by size and watching you instead. "If you are buying, **the price is on the wall**. If you are selling, put it on the scale. If you are admiring, admire from the door; the sparks have opinions."

choices.unavailableNote: You have no tin, and she does not buy the idea of tin.

again-tin.text:
She remembers the weight before she remembers your face.

"More tin? **Put it on the scale**. Do not tell me it is good; the scale decides." The girl has stopped sorting and is watching the pan, and Ada does not tell her to look away. "You can watch," she says, to the girl. "You will be weighing it yourself soon enough."

choices.unavailableNote: You have no tin, and she does not buy the idea of tin.

choices.text: Ask what is on the bench now.

again-word.text:
"You will not need it," she says, before you ask. "Nobody buys a tripod twice."

She is already reaching for the next piece, and the girl has taken up the small hammer to tap the charcoal loose. "If you are going to stand there, hold the light. My hands are full and the light is a child's job."

choices.text: Ask what is on the bench now.

again-work.text:
The tripod went to its man. She is starting something with a narrower neck — a blade blank, longer than her forearm — and the girl is pumping the bellows without being told.

"You again," she says. "Stand clear of the sparks or go back to the yard. And do not talk to the girl while she is counting. She loses count and then I lose my temper."

choices.text: Ask what the blade is for.
choices.unavailableNote: She has already told you, and does not repeat herself.

choices.text: Watch the blade until it cools.
choices.unavailableNote: You have already watched one blade cool. She will not make a second performance of it.

blade.text:
"A votive," she says. "Someone promised a blade to a goddess and then did not want to give up a good one. So I make a bad one beautifully."

She turns the blank over. "That is most of my work, if you want the truth of it. The good blades go to men who will use them and never think of me. The beautiful bad ones go to the goddess, and she does not write."

tin.text: She weighs it in her hand, then on the scale, then in her hand again. "Good tin. Not the gray stuff." The silver comes out of a jar and not from under the floor, which is a courtesy. "**Tell the yard you sold to Ada**. They will not believe you, but it will make them ask."

work.text: "A tripod for a man who will never use it. He wants it to look like the one his father had." She turns the piece. "The island word for this is not a word I can write. So I make it and he calls it what he likes. My father would have called it something worse, and charged more."

choices.text: Ask what the islanders call it.

word.text: She says it twice, slowly, and then laughs at your face. "You will not need it. Nobody buys a tripod twice." The girl says it again, quieter, and Ada pretends not to hear, which is how you know she is pleased.

watched.text:
The blade goes from yellow to straw to a dull gray that is not a color so much as a decision. Ada turns it once, tests the edge against her thumb, and sets it in the rack.

“There,” she says. “Now you have seen the whole of it. The rest is the same work, and the same hands, and nobody watches twice.” She takes up the next blank. “Go and sell something.”

choices.text: Leave her to the next piece.

provenance.notes: Ada and the workshop are invented; copper and tin working on the island is attested.

scene.goal: Sell the tin without being cheated
scene.obstacle: Ada's scale and her daughter's eyes
scene.turn: She lets the girl watch the weighing
